entry: Popular name for the 1920s, a decade of economic prosperity and cultural change in Western society, particularly the United States. In France the decade was known as the *années folles* ('crazy years'). [[Jazz]] blossomed, the flapper redefined the modern look for British and American women, and [[Art Deco]] peaked. Automobiles, moving pictures, radio and electrical appliances reached millions of people, and mass-market advertising drove consumer demand. In many countries, women won the right to vote. The [[Wall Street crash of 1929]] ended the era, and the [[Great Depression]] brought years of hardship worldwide.

American filmmaker and actor, born in New York City to actors Estelle and [[Carl Reiner]]. He rose to prominence as Michael "Meathead" Stivic in *All in the Family* before turning to directing. His films include *This Is Spinal Tap* (1984), *Stand by Me* (1986), *The Princess Bride* (1987) and *When Harry Met Sally...* (1989). A progressive political activist, he co-founded the American Foundation for Equal Rights with his wife, Michele. He and Michele were found stabbed to death in their [[Los Angeles]] home; their son has been indicted on two counts of first-degree murder.

[[Crime]] of taking or attempting to take anything of value by force, threat of force, or fear. Under [[Common law|common law]], it is a larceny or [[Theft|theft]] accomplished by an [[Assault|assault]], with intent to deprive the owner permanently. Robbery is distinguished from other theft, such as burglary, shoplifting or pickpocketing, by its inherently violent nature; in jurisdictions that distinguish felonies from misdemeanors, it is always a felony. Types include armed robbery, which involves a [[Weapon|weapon]]; aggravated robbery, involving a deadly weapon or something that appears to be one; highway robbery or mugging, which occurs in public places such as sidewalks and streets; and carjacking, stealing a car from a victim by force. In [[England]] and [[Wales]], robbery is a statutory offense under the Theft Act 1968 and is triable only on indictment. In Canada, the Criminal Code makes it an indictable offense with a maximum penalty of life imprisonment.

English singer and songwriter. He found fame as a member of the pop group Take That before launching a solo career. His three concerts at Knebworth in 2003 drew over 375,000 people. His discography includes seven UK No. 1 singles, and he has sold an estimated 75 million to 80 million records worldwide. He has received a record 18 Brit Awards. He rejoined Take That in 2010 for the album *Progress*, and the film *Better Man* (2024) is based on his life.

American [[Science fiction|science fiction]] author, engineer and naval [[Officer (armed forces)|officer]]. Sometimes called the "dean of science fiction writers", he was among the first to emphasize scientific accuracy in his fiction and was a pioneer of hard science fiction. With [[Isaac Asimov]] and [[Arthur C. Clarke]], he was considered one of the "Big Three" of English-language science fiction. Notable works include *Stranger in a Strange Land*, *Starship Troopers* and *The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress*. His fiction repeatedly addressed [[Liberty|individual liberty]], self-reliance and the tendency of society to repress nonconformist thought. Some works drew controversy for plural marriage and [[Militarism|militarism]]. He won four Hugo Awards for novels and was named the first Science Fiction Writers Grand Master in 1974. He coined terms that entered the [[English language]], including *grok* and *waldo*, and popularized "TANSTAAFL" and "pay it forward".

British Army officer and founder of the [[Scouting|Scout movement]]. He defended the town of Mafeking during the [[Second Boer War]] in 1899. In 1907 he held an experimental camp on Brownsea Island, and his book *Scouting for Boys* (1908) helped spread the movement. He retired from the army in 1910 to form The Scout Association, and with his sister Agnes he founded The Girl Guides Association that year. He married Olave St Clair Soames in 1912 and guided both associations until retiring in 1937. He spent his last years in Nyeri, Kenya, where he died and was buried; his grave is a national monument. MI5 files released in 2010 show that in 1937 he met the German ambassador Joachim von Ribbentrop in London and was invited to meet [[Adolf Hitler]], though there is no evidence that the meeting took place.

Anglo-Irish [[Chemistry|chemist]] and physicist, largely regarded as the first modern chemist. He was also a pioneer of the experimental [[Scientific method|scientific method]]. He moved to [[Oxford]] in 1654 to pursue his work more successfully. He is best known for [[Boyle's law]], which describes the inversely proportional relationship between the pressure and volume of a gas kept at constant temperature in a closed system. He demonstrated it in air pump experiments with [[Robert Hooke]]. His book *The Sceptical Chymist* is seen as a cornerstone of chemistry. A devout Anglican, he published extensively on topics from hydrostatics to [[Theology|theology]] and was a founding fellow of the Royal Society in 1660.

French filmmaker known for an ascetic, minimalist style. He used non-professional actors, whom he called models, along with ellipses and sparse scoring. Captured by the Germans in 1940, he was held as a [[Prisoner of war|prisoner of war]] for more than a year, an experience that informed *A Man Escaped* (1956). In a career spanning five decades he made only 13 feature films, a reflection of his painstaking approach and non-commercial preoccupations. In *Notes on the Cinematographer* (1975) he argued for [[Cinematography|cinematography]] as a new language of moving images and sounds. Seven of his films appeared in the 2012 *Sight and Sound* critics' poll of the greatest films, and *A Man Escaped*, *Pickpocket* (1959) and *Au hasard Balthazar* (1966) were ranked among the top 100. [[Jean-Luc Godard]] wrote, "He is the French cinema, as Dostoevsky is the Russian novel and Mozart is German music."

Scottish poet and lyricist, widely regarded as the national poet of [[Scotland]]. He wrote in the [[Scots language|Scots]] dialect and in standard English, and he is regarded as a pioneer of the Romantic movement. After his death he inspired the founders of both [[Liberalism|liberalism]] and [[Socialism|socialism]], and he became a cultural icon in Scotland and among the Scottish diaspora. He collected folk songs from across Scotland, often revising or adapting them. His poem and song "[[Auld Lang Syne]]" (1788) is often sung at Hogmanay, and "Scots Wha Hae" (1793) served for a long time as an unofficial [[National anthem|national anthem]]. In 2009 he was chosen as the greatest Scot in a vote run by STV.

American [[Organic chemistry|organic chemist]], considered by many the preeminent synthetic organic chemist of the 20th century. He received the [[Nobel Prize]] in Chemistry in 1965 for his achievements in the art of organic synthesis. Woodward used ultraviolet spectroscopy to devise rules for determining molecular structures, and he determined the structures of penicillin and terramycin. In 1944, during [[World War II]], he reported the synthesis of the alkaloid [[Quinine|quinine]], a treatment for [[Malaria]]. His later total syntheses included strychnine (1954), reserpine (1956) and, with Albert Eschenmoser, [[Vitamin B12|vitamin B12]] (1973), then the most complex non-protein biomolecule known at the time. With Roald Hoffmann he formulated the Woodward-Hoffmann rules (1965), which explain pericyclic reactions through orbital [[Symmetry|symmetry]]. He remained at [[Harvard University]] for the rest of his life.

British military officer and first British governor of the [[Bengal]] Presidency, also known as Clive of India. He began as a clerk for the [[East India Company]] and joined its private army after the fall of Madras. He is credited with establishing Company rule in Bengal by winning the Battle of Plassey in 1757. In return for supporting the Nawab Mir Jafar, he was guaranteed a jagir of £90,000 a year. When he left India in 1767 his fortune was £401,102, which he remitted through the [[Dutch East India Company]]. Back in Britain he used his Indian wealth to obtain an Irish barony and a seat in Parliament. His actions made him one of Britain's most controversial colonial figures, though he worked only as an agent of the East India Company, not of the British government.

American actor and producer, widely regarded as one of the greatest actors of his generation. He won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for *The Godfather Part II* (1974), becoming the first male to win for an Italian-language performance, and the Academy Award for Best Actor for *Raging Bull* (1980). He worked often with [[Martin Scorsese]], and he was further nominated for *Taxi Driver* and *The Deer Hunter*. In 1989 he co-founded TriBeCa Productions with Jane Rosenthal, and the two founded the Tribeca Film Festival in 2002. He directed *A Bronx Tale* (1993) and *The Good Shepherd* (2006), and he portrayed [[Bernie Madoff]] in the [[HBO]] film *The Wizard of Lies* (2017).

American actor and producer whose leading films have grossed over $14.3 billion worldwide. He earned a BAFTA Award for playing [[Charlie Chaplin]] in *Chaplin* (1992). After drug-related arrests he entered court-ordered rehabilitation and has remained sober since 2003. He revitalized his career as [[Iron Man]] in ten [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]] films, and he won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for *Oppenheimer* (2023). He was the highest-paid actor in the world annually from 2013 to 2015.

American actor and filmmaker. He won the Academy Award for Best Actor for playing an alcoholic former [[Country music|country music]] star in *Tender Mercies* (1983). He was Oscar-nominated for *The Godfather* (1972) and *Apocalypse Now* (1979), and his feature debut was a brief role as Boo Radley in *To Kill a Mockingbird* (1962). Duvall won two Primetime Emmy Awards for the AMC limited series *Broken Trail* (2006). Critic Vincent Canby dubbed him "the American Olivier" in 1980, and the label stuck.

Confederate general who commanded the Army of Northern Virginia from 1862 to 1865. A top graduate of the [[United States Military Academy]], he distinguished himself in the [[Mexican–American War]] and was superintendent of the academy. Lee said he opposed slavery in principle, but he supported its legality and enslaved hundreds. He won many battles against larger Union armies, but he was defeated at [[Battle of Gettysburg|Gettysburg]] in 1863. He surrendered to [[Ulysses S. Grant]] at Appomattox Court House in April 1865. After the war he supported reconciliation as president of Washington College.

American lawyer and [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] politician. He served as the 64th U.S. attorney general from 1961 to 1964 and as a U.S. senator from New York until his assassination. The brother of [[John F. Kennedy]], he advocated civil rights and fought [[Organized crime|organized crime]] as attorney general. In the Senate he opposed U.S. involvement in the [[Vietnam War]] and sponsored legislation to address [[Poverty|poverty]] in blighted communities. He was a leading Democratic presidential candidate when he was shot after winning the California primary. He died the following day, and [[Sirhan Sirhan]] was convicted of the killing.

British [[Royal Navy|naval officer]] and Antarctic explorer. He led the Discovery Expedition of 1901–1904, which set a southern record by marching to latitude 82°S and discovered the Antarctic Plateau. On the Terra Nova Expedition (1910–1913), a party of five he led reached the [[South Pole]] in January 1912, less than five weeks after Amundsen's expedition. On the return journey a planned meeting with supporting dog teams failed, and Scott and his companions died. The first Antarctic [[Fossil|fossils]] found, with their bodies, came from the *Glossopteris* tree and showed that Antarctica had once been forested. Scott was hailed as a hero after his death, but later criticism questioned his competence and character, and 21st-century commentators have regarded him more positively.

American poet known for realistic depictions of rural [[New England]] life and his command of colloquial American speech. Born in San Francisco, he grew up in Lawrence, Massachusetts. He is the only poet to have won four [[Pulitzer Prize|Pulitzer Prizes]] for Poetry. He was appointed United States Poet Laureate in 1958, received the Congressional Gold Medal in 1960 and was named poet laureate of Vermont in 1961. His poems often examine complex social and philosophical themes through ordinary rural settings, such as "Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening" and "Mending Wall." His father named him after [[Robert E. Lee]], and in 1961 Frost recited his poetry at the inauguration of [[John F. Kennedy]].

American engineer and inventor. In 1807 his *North River Steamboat*, also called *Clermont*, carried passengers on the [[Hudson River]] from [[New York City]] to Albany and back, a round trip of 300 nautical miles completed in 62 hours. Widely credited as the developer of the world's first commercially successful [[Steamship|steamboat]], he changed river traffic and trade on major American rivers. Fulton spent about twenty years in Europe, where he worked on canals and steam-powered vessels. In 1800 [[Napoleon]] commissioned him to design a [[Submarine|submarine]], and the resulting *Nautilus* was the first practical submarine in history. Fulton is also credited with some of the earliest naval [[Torpedo|torpedoes]] for the [[Royal Navy]].

Norman adventurer who became Duke of [[Apulia]] and [[Calabria]] and conquered much of southern Italy in the 11th century. The sixth son of Tancred de Hauteville, he arrived in Italy as a mercenary and rose through cunning tactics. In 1059 Pope Nicholas II made him duke and lord of [[Sicily]]. He captured [[Bari]] in 1071, ending Byzantine dominance in the region. In 1084 he rescued [[Pope Gregory VII]] from Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV. In 1081 he invaded the [[Byzantine Empire]], taking [[Corfu]] and Dyrrhachium, but his death from a fever halted further advances. His conquests paved the way for the [[Kingdom of Sicily]] under his nephew Roger II.

American physicist and inventor, one of the founding fathers of modern [[Spaceflight|rocketry]]. He and his team launched 34 rockets between 1926 and 1941, reaching altitudes as high as 2.6 km (1.6 mi) and speeds as fast as 885 km/h (550 mph). On March 16, 1926, he launched the world's first liquid-fueled rocket. Goddard held 214 [[Patent|patents]], including ones for a multi-stage rocket and a liquid-fuel rocket in 1914. He pioneered two-axis control using [[Gyroscope|gyroscopes]] and steerable thrust. Despite little public or financial support and ridicule from the press, he recognized early the potential of rockets for ballistic missiles and space travel. The Goddard Space Flight Center of [[NASA]] was named in his honor in 1959.

American [[Federal Bureau of Investigation|FBI]] agent who spied for the [[Soviet Union]] and later Russia. Intermittently from 1979 to 2001, he sold about six thousand classified documents to the [[KGB]], detailing U.S. nuclear war strategies and counterintelligence. Some KGB agents he exposed were executed. The Justice Department called his espionage "possibly the worst intelligence disaster in U.S. history." He was arrested in February 2001 after leaving classified materials at a dead drop in Virginia. He pleaded guilty to espionage and conspiracy and received 15 consecutive life sentences without parole. He remained imprisoned until his death.

English [[Polymath|polymath]], active as a physicist, astronomer, geologist and architect. He began as an assistant to [[Robert Boyle]], and he built the vacuum pumps used in Boyle's gas experiments. In *Micrographia* (1665) he coined the term [[Cell (biology)|cell]] and encouraged microscopic investigation. He inferred a wave theory of light and identified the rotations of Mars and Jupiter. He arguably was the first to propose that gravity obeys an inverse square law, a priority that fed his rivalry with [[Isaac Newton]]. He identified fossils as the remains of organisms, including extinct species, which presaged 19th-century arguments for [[Evolution|evolution]]. After the [[Great Fire of London]] he surveyed property lines and helped rebuild the city, and he was the first Curator of Experiments of the Royal Society.

American [[Blues|blues]] musician and songwriter, regarded as a master of the Delta blues style. His recording career spanned only seven months, during which he made two sessions, in San Antonio in 1936 and Dallas in 1937, producing 29 songs. Most were released as singles in 1937 and 1938, and [[Columbia Records]] later bought the recordings. Little was known of his life, which gave rise to legends, including the tale that he sold his soul to the devil at a crossroads. The 1961 album *King of the Delta Blues Singers* brought his work to a wider audience. [[Eric Clapton]] called him "the most important blues singer that ever lived", and [[Keith Richards]] and [[Robert Plant]] also cited his influence. The [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] describes him as perhaps "the first ever rock star."

German physician and [[Microbiology|microbiologist]]. He won the 1905 [[Nobel Prize]] in Physiology or Medicine for his work on [[Tuberculosis]]. He identified the specific causative agents of [[Anthrax]], tuberculosis and [[Cholera]], and he is regarded as one of the main founders of modern bacteriology. He showed that germs "could cause a specific disease", providing proof for the germ theory and the scientific basis of public health. Koch's postulates, four principles for linking pathogens to specific diseases, remain in use in most situations. He is popularly nicknamed the father of microbiology, along with [[Louis Pasteur]]. His culture method used agar and glass plates, later developed into the Petri dish by his assistant Julius Richard Petri. Tuberculin, which he introduced as a medication for tuberculosis, proved ineffective but was later developed for diagnosis.
